papers.title: Deciphering lung microbial EV pneumotypes in acute respiratory distress syndrome proteome wide
papers.abstract: Background. Pneumotypes hold potential predictive value for pathogenesis, outcomes, and interventions. Lung microbiome releases extracellular vesicles (EVs). However, EV-derived pneumotypes in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) have not been studied yet. Objectives. We aimed to identify pneumotypes in ARDS patients by comprehensively profiling lung microbiome-released EV proteins in bronchioalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Methods. We extracted EVs from 106 participants (57 cases and 49 healthy controls) enrolled in the ARDSNet and SPIROMICS clinical trials and subjected to nanoparticle liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to create microbial metaproteomics. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified by Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and spectral clustering of these DEPs was utilized to reveal patterns in microbial EV protein profiles. The association between pneumotypes and the disease was assessed. Pneumotype-associated DEPs were identified using logistic regression, and their functional annotation was performed based on the eggNOG 5 database. The taxonomy of lung microbes was determined at the species-level and ranked by biomass contributions. Results. Ninety DEPs were identified in ARDS lavage samples (53 upregulated and 37 downregulated) compared with healthy controls. There were five pneumotypes, namely, P1, P2, P3, P4, and P5, identified by clustering the differentially expressed microbial EV proteins. Few pneumotype-associated DEPs were shared among these pneumotypes and mainly correlated with ARDS etiology and organ functions. The significant difference in mortality was observed in P3 and P4 subtypes. In contrast, all patients in P1 and P5 subgroups survived. Patients in P2 and P3 groups experienced a significant reduction in both of central nervous system (CNS) failure-free days and the days without organ failure compared with other subgroups. Besides, patients in P3 and P4 exhibited a higher prevalence of baseline shock and hypertension, greater use of vasopressors or inotropes within the previous 24 hours, higher positive end-expiratory pressure during ventilation, and lower body temperature and hematocrit levels. Alpha and beta diversity analyses showed significant shifts in P2 patients. The taxonomy of the top-ranked microbes exhibited different pathogens in P2, P3, and P4. Conclusions. This study, for the first time, identified five EV expression patterns of lung microbiota in the BALF of ARDS patients. These intrinsically featured EV pneumotypes in the lung are associated with mortality, etiology, lung functions, medication administration, and disease severity in ARDS patients.

papers.title: Toxoplasma gondii-induced NETs are mediated by CR3 engagement and the vital non-lytic NETosis pathway
papers.abstract: Approximately one-third of the global human population harbors an infection with the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. The immune system exploits neutrophils and one of their effector mechanisms, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), as an attempt to capture and neutralize T. gondii. NETs, composed of DNA, myeloperoxidase, citrullinated histone 3, and elastase, play a dual role in pathogen entrapment and amplification of the immune response. Traditionally, NET release was considered to result in neutrophil cell death. However, studies have identified an alternative process, vital NETosis, that allows NET formation while maintaining cell viability. Although T. gondii induces NET formation, the associated molecular mechanisms are not fully understood, and the neutrophil fate is unknown. In this study, the promyelocytic cell line HL-60 was differentiated into neutrophil-like cells (NLCs) and infected with type I (RH) or type II (PA7) T. gondii. Extracellular DNA was found in increasing concentrations over time in both type 1 and type 2 T. gondii-infected NLCs. Immunofluorescence staining for DNA and citrullinated histone 3 at 4, 6, and 16 hours post-infection confirmed NET formation by confocal microscopy. Cell viability at 16 hours post-infection was assessed by live/dead staining and extracellular ATP measurement, revealing that most NET-releasing neutrophils retained membrane integrity, consistent with vital NETosis. Additionally, immunofluorescence microscopy at 15 and 30 minutes further confirmed the fast release of nuclear DNA, a hallmark of vital NETosis. The use of opsonin-containing human serum and an anti-CD11b blocking antibody identified complement receptor 3 (CR3) as a receptor mediating T. gondii-induced vital NETosis. These findings demonstrate that T. gondii triggers vital NETosis in neutrophils through a CR3-dependent mechanism, advancing our understanding of the innate immune response to this globally prevalent parasite and laying the groundwork for future investigations into the molecular pathways that may be therapeutically targeted to support neutrophil-mediated immunity during infection.

papers.title: Strain-resolved metagenomics shows gut microbiome signatures in a case-control study of Malawian children with zoonotic schistosomiasis
papers.abstract: In 2024, Mangochi District, Malawi, we identified unexpected cases of zoonotic schistosomiasis associated with faecal egg excretion of Schistosoma haematobium, Schistosoma mattheei and hybrids thereof (S. haematobium x S. mattheei). Schistosomiasis is associated with gut microbiome alterations, but these associations remain unexplored in zoonotic schistosomiasis. Whether people with schistosomiasis are colonised with more closely related gut bacterial strains than people without schistosomiasis is also unclear. To better understand these patterns, we conducted a case-control study, using strain-resolved metagenomics to analyse faecal samples from 36 children: 12 with zoonotic schistosomiasis (S. haematobium and S. mattheei), 12 with "classic" urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium only) and 12 uninfected controls. Microbial diversity, taxonomic composition, metabolic pathways and antimicrobial resistance gene profiles did not differ significantly between groups. However, Brachyspira, particularly Brachyspira aalborgi - an organism often associated with intestinal spirochaetosis - was more abundant in children with zoonotic schistosomiasis. We found no evidence of closely related B. aalborgi strains shared between participants, suggesting that localised B. aalborgi transmission networks are unlikely to explain the enrichment. In contrast, phylogenetic profiling across 143 other bacterial species revealed greater strain similarity between the gut microbiomes of children with any type of schistosomiasis than between those of controls. Broadly, we demonstrate the scientific value of strain-resolved metagenomics for investigating linked bacterial and schistosome exposures where local water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure is inadequate. Future inclusion of livestock and environmental samples could be used to better identify where transmission pathways overlap, providing evidence to inform integrated disease surveillance and control.

papers.title: Dynamic interactions of the coronavirus PEDV nucleoprotein with its viral partner nsp3 and RNA
papers.abstract: Summary While coronavirus genome replication and transcription occur inside double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) in infected cells, nucleocapsid assembly of genomic RNA takes place at their cytoplasmic (external) face. Neosynthesized viral mRNAs (including genomic RNA) are exported from the DMV through nsp3/nsp4 pores and genomic RNAs are believed to be selected for encapsidation through an essential interaction of the nucleoprotein N with the amino-terminal domain of nsp3. Here, we describe the interaction play between the N of porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV, an alphacoronavirus) with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 and with RNAs. While N interacts with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 with a dissociation constant (KD) of about 150 nM, it binds to diverse small RNAs, displaying an affinity in the pM range for a short RNA (RNA[8mer]). This RNA and a 60-nt long RNA hairpin were both able to fully displace nsp3 complexed with N. In contrast, nsp3 was not able to dissociate RNA from N-RNA complexes. Using truncated forms of N and of the N-ter domain of nsp3, we showed that the RNA binding site does not fully overlap the nsp3 binding site on N. These results suggest that the interaction play between N, nsp3 and RNA is unidirectional, allowing to propose a mechanistical model for genome encapsidation, model in which N is first recruited by nsp3 at the cytoplasmic face of the DMV to bind to nucleotide stretches of (genomic) RNA exiting from the nsp3/nsp4 channel and concomitantly to dissociate from nsp3.

papers.title: CurveKinetix: A user-friendly application for analysis of biological time series data
papers.abstract: Of interest to many biologists is how organisms change over time: their growth, their response to a stimulus, their movement. How quickly a process starts, accelerates, slows, or changes direction, often carries critical biological information for hypothesis testing. Extraction of these parameters, however, requires computational expertise or reliance on existing software not designed for the needed analysis. We present here CurveKinetix, a graphical user interface application that helps researchers extract quantitative parameters from time series data without writing code. Users can quickly go from instrument data files to estimation of parameters using three complementary methods to visualized data customization and export. We exhibit CurveKinetix's utility in two case studies. In the first, we show expression of an operon correlates with slowing of population level growth. In the second, we enumerate viral fusion dynamics, demonstrating CurveKinetixs framework can be applied to a range of biological questions. By making flexible quantitative analysis straightforward, CurveKinetix helps experimentalists extract more information from their data and supports clearer, more rigorous interpretation of time-resolved experiments.

papers.title: Olfactory epithelium local proteomic during SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters
papers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 has been extensively studied since its recent emergence. It has proven to be an excellent model of respiratory virus impact on nasal epithelium for its massive impact notably on the olfactory epithelium using the hamster animal model. We and others have previously observed that following infection, the nasal epithelium is massively infiltrated by innate immune cells followed by desquamation leading to release of cellular debris in the lumen of the nasal cavity. This impact varies spatially in the nasal cavity, the anterior part being infected early mainly in the respiratory epithelium followed by the olfactory epithelium in the posterior part. In order to better understand the impact on host cells, we decided to use laser microdissection to analyse the proteomic of restricted area of infected epithelium taking into account this spatial variation. We observed that protein levels are mostly decreased following SARS-CoV-2 infection at 2 days post-infection which contrasts with many genes having a stable expression level. Using available scRNASeq library, we could associate the variation of protein levels to the various cell types of the nasal cavity epithelium and our findings are consistent with a destruction of most epithelial cells and the infiltration of innate immune cells. Overall, our study confirms that SARS-CoV-2-host interactions lead to profound alteration of genes expression and that while most studies heavily rely on mRNA levels, it may be decorrelated to protein levels. Our approach offers an alternative to study host-virus interactions using spatially restricted proteomic.

papers.title: Calcium Signaling and Glycerol-3-Phosphate Metabolism Coordinate Extracellular Vesicle Biogenesis in Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly recognized as important mediators of fungal physiology and host-pathogen interactions, but the mechanisms governing their biogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we combined time-course RNA sequencing with genome-wide genetic screening to define the regulatory network controlling EV production in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. Transcriptomic analysis identified an EV-associated regulon enriched in genes involved in vesicular trafficking, cell wall remodeling, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function and ion homeostasis. Our screen further identified diverse regulators of EV production, highlighting endosomal trafficking, mitochondrial metabolism and calcium homeostasis. Cell viability was only weakly associated with EV production, arguing against cell lysis as the primary mechanism of EV release. Genetic and pharmacological analyses established calcium-dependent calcineurin signalling as a major regulator of EV production. We identified the calcineurin target Had1 as a positive regulator of EV production and demonstrate that Had1 functions as a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase. Loss of HAD1 caused glycerol-3-phosphate accumulation and extensive remodeling of cellular phospholipids, accompanied by a marked reduction in EV production. Together, these findings identify a calcium-calcineurin-Had1 pathway linking intracellular signalling and lipid homeostasis to fungal EV biogenesis.

papers.title: Global evolutionary and spatiotemporal transmission dynamics of human respiroviruses and orthorubulaviruses
papers.abstract: Human parainfluenza viruses (HPIVs) cause recurrent epidemics and are a major cause of hospitalization worldwide. However, the evolutionary and transmission dynamics driving HPIV persistence remain unclear. We analysed 1,161 archived samples representing four HPIV types from seven countries using genomic sequencing and Bayesian phylodynamic inference. We show that Respirovirus (HRV-1 and HRV-3) displayed greater fluctuations in genetic diversity whereas Orthorubulavirus (HOV-2 and HOV-4) showed more gradual changes. Despite comparable evolutionary rates, the four HPIV types exhibited contrasting lineage dynamics. HRV-1 showed prolonged lineage persistence, HRV-3 underwent greater lineage turnover, and HOV-2 and HOV-4 maintained fewer co-circulating lineages. Positive selection was more pronounced in respiroviruses, particularly in the phosphoprotein gene, while positively selected sites overlapped predicted hemagglutinin-neuraminidase B-cell epitopes. Phylogeographic analyses revealed repeated interregional introductions, bidirectional transmission, and regional persistence exceeding a decade for some lineages. These findings identify distinct evolutionary and transmission dynamics underlying HPIV persistence and inform the development of broadly protective vaccines and therapeutics.

papers.title: A tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine elicits superior protective immunity over licensed acellular pertussis vaccine against emerging antibiotic-resistant variants
papers.abstract: Pertussis remains a major global health burden and has been resurging rapidly over the past decade. The causes of pertussis re-emergence are multifactorial, including vaccine-induced pathogen evolution, antimicrobial resistance, and crucially suboptimal protective immunity elicited by the widely used acellular pertussis vaccine (aPV). In this study, we developed a tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine formulated with lipid nanoparticle (LNP), designated mPervax, which encodes inactive pertussis toxin subunit 1 (PTS1), truncated filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) and pertactin (PRN). Compared to a commercialized Tetanus-diptheria-pertussis vaccine Boostrix, mPervax induced stronger and broader innate immune activation, superior antigen-specific Th1-type CD4+ T and Tfh cell responses, and robust B. pertussis-specific antibody responses with remarkably increased magnitude and functionality. In addition, mPervax conferred an efficient maternal antibody-mediated protection in offspring mice and reshaped the immune profile established by primary Boostrix immunization towards a Th1-phenotype when used as a heterologous booster. Furthermore, upon bacterial challenge, mPervax outperformed Boostrix not only against the WHO reference strain 18323, but strikingly provided effective protection against emerging antibiotic-resistant clinical isolates that are deficient in PRN and/or FHA. Collectively, these data demonstrate that the mRNA pertussis vaccine is superior to Boostrix in multiple contexts, and therefore holds promise for next-generation pertussis vaccine development.

papers.title: Elucidating and Overcoming Lignin-Mediated Growth Suppression in Anaerobic Fungi
papers.abstract: Native to the gastrointestinal tract of herbivores, anaerobic gut fungi (AGF) (Neocallimastigomycetes) have evolved highly efficient enzymatic machinery for lignocellulose degradation. While AGF are capable of degrading lignocellulose, they more readily degrade its cellulose and hemicellulose components. Lignin is the most recalcitrant component of lignocellulose that serves as both structural support and a microbial defense strategy within plants. In this study, a negative correlation between AGF growth and substrate lignin content was quantified, ranging from pure cellulose to the lignin-rich substrate eucalyptus. Based on this observation, we investigated the impact of lignin on AGF viability and concluded that lignin delayed and slowed AGF?s growth trajectory, with IC50 ranging from 10.7 ? 16.3 mg/mL, and specifically that lignin-rich substrates decreased overall growth. Meanwhile, lignin acted as an AGF deterrent, likely by preventing access to essential sugar-based polymers and lowering overall nutrient bioavailability. However, AGF growth was restored following glucose supplementation on otherwise growth-limiting woody substrates. Through experimental, sequential serial batch culture challenge, we successfully adapted one strain of AGF (Neocallimastix californiae) to grow on lignin-rich eucalyptus. This study supports the industrial valorization of lignocellulose using AGF by elucidating the relationship between the major bottleneck, lignin, on fungal growth. It also provides a strategy for optimizing fungal strains selected for growth in nutrient-deficient and lignin-rich environments.

papers.title: Genome-Wide Association Study Identifies Novel Genetic Variants Linked to Meropenem Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae
papers.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae have emerged as an urgent public health threat in recent years. Infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae in particular are associated with high rates of mortality, especially in immunocompromised patients. Substantial carbapenem resistance remains unexplained in K. pneumoniae even after accounting for known resistance genes. To uncover unknown mechanisms associated with meropenem resistance, we performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) in 1,705 K. pneumoniae clinical isolates with previously determined resistance profiles to meropenem . We conducted the GWAS by using an elastic net regression to control for genome-wide linkage disequilibrium and combined it with a conditional linear mixed model to control for the presence of genes known to confer carbapenem resistance. The resulting set of variants predicted to be associated with meropenem resistance mapped to genes broadly related to the plasticity of the genome. We developed a visualization tool integrating GWAS results with phenotypic data and polymorphic site information to aid in hypothesis generation, which allowed us to prioritize novel genomic candidates. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the combined approach in detecting novel genomic variants associated with meropenem resistance in K. pneumoniae, while controlling for strong bacterial population structure, to advance our understanding of the genetic basis of carbapenem resistance.

papers.title: Inhibition of Bacteriophage Infection by Natural and Synthetic DNA-binding Compounds
papers.abstract: The arms race between bacteria and phages involves a wide range of immune and anti-immune systems on both sides. One of the long-known mechanisms of antiphage defense involves DNA intercalators such as daunorubicin and its analogues. Daunorubicin was also shown to inhibit bacterial growth as well as eukaryotic cell division, underlying its use in chemotherapy. Other DNA intercalators and minor groove binding dyes are widely used for nucleic acids staining, but have not been studied for their effects on viral infection. Here, we systematically investigate the effects of known intercalator and DNA-binding agents, including daunorubicin and Hoechst derivatives, on phage infection in Escherichia coli. Using a diverse panel of phages with various replication mechanisms we identify phylogenetic groups sensitive to DNA-binding dyes and determined which stage of the viral life cycle was inhibited. Our data suggest that the active antiviral compounds block early steps of infection without cells killing, arguing against an abortive infection mechanism and lethal membrane permeabilization suggested recently. Together, our results expand the list of small molecules that affect phage infection and reveal DNA binders that inhibit viral DNA entry and/or replication without affecting cell physiology.

papers.title: PAannotate: Software for Exploring Pseudomonas aeruginosa Gene-Expression Associations from Transcriptomic Data
papers.abstract: With the proliferation of transcriptomic data for Pseudomonas aeruginosa there is a need for software programs able to efficiently analyze both individual transcriptomes as well as large, publicly available compendiums of arrays. PAannotate is an R package and native macOS application capable of analyzing the Whiteley Lab database of 5,821 transcriptomes from 470 BioProjects. In the application, researchers can use recorded metadata such as strain, medium or treatment to select experiments or genes associated with particular expression patterns. Alternatively, selecting one gene of interest, a user can find other, coordinately regulated genes that move together across many environments, mutants, and treatments. PAannotate also allows users to select groups of genes and to use Gene Ontology and KEGG annotations and enrichment analysis to see whether those genes are associated with particular biological functions more often than expected by chance, determine whether a particular perturbation produces a reproducible response across studies, or find public experiments resembling your own experiment. Researchers can build and customize heatmaps and association networks. In one project, we have examined the P. aeruginosa transcriptomic associations with the genes encoding the Pf prophage present in P. aeruginosa strain PAO1. We found a strong negative correlation between PA0724, a Pf4 gene, and ccmG, a bacterial gene involved in energy metabolism. We identified that much of this relationship was reflected by a difference in whether the bacteria were grown with acetate or glycerol as their carbon source. This finding illustrates how PAannotate helps researchers investigate P. aeruginosa gene correlations.

papers.title: Salmonella MgtC promotes polymyxin B resistance and systemic infection by activating LpxO-mediated lipid A hydroxylation
papers.abstract: The intracellular pathogen Salmonella Typhimurium modifies the lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide through various lipid A-modifying enzymes, thereby acquiring resistance to host cationic antimicrobial peptides during infection. While regulation of these enzymes at the transcription level has been extensively studied, however, regulation at the activity level remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the Salmonella virulence factor MgtC interacts with LpxO, an enzyme that hydroxylates the 3'-myristoyl chain of hexa-acylated lipid A, identified through bacterial two-hybrid screening for potential MgtC interaction partners. MgtC binding to LpxO promotes lipid A hydroxylation in a concentration-dependent manner, and the Leu287 residue in the C-terminal helix of LpxO is required for this interaction. Substitution of Leu287 with Ala reduces MgtC binding without affecting intrinsic hydroxylase activity, consequently impairing MgtC-enhanced lipid A hydroxylation. This substitution decreases resistance to both the antimicrobial peptide polymyxin B and human serum, and attenuates virulence in a mouse infection model. These findings suggest that Salmonella exploits MgtC to promote LpxO hydroxylation activity, thereby enhancing survival inside the host.

papers.title: Distinct chaperones coordinate the type III secretion system assembly and effector secretion in Vibrio parahaemolyticus
papers.abstract: Many Gram-negative bacterial pathogens rely on the type III secretion system (T3SS) to deliver virulence factors or effectors into host cells. In Vibrio parahaemolyticus, the leading cause of seafood-borne gastroenteritis, one of the two T3SSs, the T3SS2, is essential for intestinal colonization and infection in the human body. While many T3SS2 effectors have been extensively characterized, the chaperones that guide their biogenesis and coordinate assembly of the T3SS machinery remain poorly understood. Here, combining comparative transcriptomic and proteomic approaches with functional analyses, we reveal that four T3SS2 chaperones exert non-overlapping control over distinct clients for pathogenesis. We further show that these chaperones form a hierarchical, multi-layered checkpoint system that ensures the temporal order of secretion, coordinating injectisome assembly, pore formation, and effector deployment. Our findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding the regulation of T3SS2, demonstrating that discrete non-redundant chaperone-mediated assembly is conserved across diverse Gram-negative pathogens.

papers.title: A microbiota-dependent fitness locus promotes intraspecies competition and cell envelope resilience in gut bacterium Phocaeicola vulgatus
papers.abstract: A central question in gut microbial ecology is how dominant bacterial species establish and occupy their niches amid inter- and intraspecies competition. Phocaeicola vulgatus (Pvu) is a Gram-negative anaerobe and prevalent member of the human gut microbiome that can integrate into established gut communities without antibiotic pretreatment, yet mechanisms underlying this competitive success remain poorly understood. Using in vivo transposon insertion sequencing, we identified a three-gene locus that promotes Pvu intraspecies fitness in the presence of a complex microbiota but is dispensable in germ-free hosts. The locus encodes a predicted HU/IHF superfamily histone-like DNA-binding protein (DifH), a hypothetical lipid-binding protein (DifS), and a FadL-like outer-membrane transporter (DifT). In vitro genetic and transcriptomic analyses implicated these genes in cell envelope resilience. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing revealed that DifH binds a specific repetitive DNA motif at its own locus and a limited set of additional loci involved in metabolism, envelope biogenesis, and cellular defense. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized fitness locus that promotes cell envelope resilience, enables intraspecies competition, and supports Pvu persistence within complex gut microbial communities. More broadly, these results uncover mechanisms by which this dominant gut commensal secures its niche and suggests avenues to therapeutically modulate gut microbiota composition.

papers.title: Phage integrons are vaults of privatized counterdefense genes
papers.abstract: Integrons facilitate the adaptation of microbes by capturing beneficial gene cassettes, including antiphage defense systems, but their role in phage adaptation remains unclear. Here, we identify reversed integron cassette organization in phages, with 96% of reverse-oriented cassettes lacking detectable homologs in surveyed bacterial and plasmid integrons. Phage cassettes are enriched in counterdefenses, including viral sponge-like proteins. Despite these differences, representative phage and bacterial integron integrases recombine cassette attachment sites from either source; however, exchange between oppositely organized phage and bacterial integron arrays misorients incoming gene cassettes relative to the recipient integron's promoter, posing an expression barrier. These findings establish integrons as a shared engine of the phage-host arms race, capturing defenses in bacteria and counterdefenses in phages, while cassette orientation buffers exchange between the two adaptive repertoires.

papers.title: Acquisition of phthiocerol dimycocerosates enabled extension of fused mycomembranes for cellular cording in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and its pathogenic relative Mycobacterium marinum form virulence-associated serpentine cords. Using live imaging and cryo-electron tomography, we show that cording involves extensive outer membrane enmeshment, such that adjacent cells share a single outer membrane. Importantly, analysis of diverse non-cording Mycobacteriales species, including the poorly virulent saprophyte M. smegmatis, reveals some membrane enmeshment in the clumped colonies. Our analyses suggest that cording was acquired in two evolutionary steps. First, acquisition of the mycolic acid-rich envelope in Mycobacteriales enabled daughter cell membranes to fuse during division, generating membrane-connected clonal clumps. Subsequent acquisition of the virulence-associated outer membrane lipids phthiocerol dimycocerosates (PDIM) facilitated more extensive membrane fusion into cords. We show that PDIM moves freely through the continuous shared outer membranes of cords. Moreover, these in vitro observations of fused membranes in M. marinum were seen during zebrafish infection. Thus, mycobacterial cording relies on an ancestral fusion-based community architecture that PDIM refined into virulence-promoting cords.

papers.title: PL25_M23: Salt-enhanced antibacterial activity of a plasmid-encoded SLT-M23 hydrolase from Virgibacillus salarius against Gram-positive bacteria
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance has intensified interest in peptidoglycan hydrolases as potential alternatives to conventional antibiotics. However, halophilic and halotolerant bacteria remain underexplored sources of these enzymes. Here, we characterized PL25_M23, a predicted 370-amino-acid, dual-domain cell wall hydrolase encoded on a candidate closed circular plasmid from Virgibacillus salarius PL25, a halotolerant Gram-positive isolate. PL25_M23 combines an N-terminal Slt35/lysozyme-like glycoside hydrolase fold with a C-terminal Peptidase_M23 domain containing the canonical HxxxD and HxH Zn2+-binding motifs characteristic of the M23 family. Although its closest characterized homolog, CwlP, shares limited sequence identity with PL25_M23, AlphaFold2 modeling and domain-restricted structural superposition support a CwlP-like, two-domain architecture. The predicted protein surface is enriched in acidic residues, a compositional feature commonly reported in halophilic proteins. Recombinant PL25_M23 reduced the viable counts of seven Gram-positive strains representing four genera, including methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, by approximately 1.9-3.8 log10 CFU/mL at a concentration of 100 &microg/mL within 60 min. EDTA treatment reduced PL25_M23 activity, whereas Zn2+ supplementation restored antibacterial activity, resulting in reductions of 1.4-3.6 log10 CFU/mL and indicating that its antibacterial activity is sensitive to metal chelation. The extent of bacterial killing increased with NaCl supplementation in all salt-tolerant test strains, with an increase of 1.4 log10 CFU/mL. Together, these findings identify PL25_M23 as a divergent, plasmid-encoded hydrolase with antibacterial activity against the Gram-positive strains tested and establish it as a candidate for further biochemical characterization and evaluation as an enzybiotic.

papers.title: Lateral interactions between antiparallel filaments drive self-assembly of the FtsZ ring in bacterial cell division
papers.abstract: The Z-ring is the organiser of cell division in most archaea and bacteria, arriving early at mid-cell and recruiting downstream proteins. While FtsZ protofilaments and their treadmilling dynamics are well understood, how FtsZ assembles into condensed Z-rings remains unknown. Here we determined the Escherichia coli in-cell electron cryotomography (cryo-ET) structure of FtsZ to 6.9 [A] resolution, showing antiparallel double filaments with the C-terminus facing the membrane. Electron cryomicroscopy (cryo-EM) of purified E. coli FtsZ showed these double filaments self-assemble. Cryo-ET of cells showed ordering of FtsZ doublets into bands, which we revealed is regulated by the disordered N-terminal residues. Structures of purified Bacillus subtilis and Thermotoga maritima FtsZ demonstrated that antiparallel lateral interactions are a conserved feature. We describe how self-assembly of the Z-ring occurs through two types of lateral interactions and propose a new role for FtsZ treadmilling in reorganising antiparallel lateral interactions during cell constriction.

papers.title: An RNase bacterial toxin family cleaves the anticodon loop across diverse tRNA isotypes
papers.abstract: Characterized bacterial tRNase toxins typically recognize individual tRNAs or restricted tRNA subsets. Here, we identify TloR (tRNA loop-targeting RNase), a tRNase with an unusually broad substrate range but a strong positional preference for exposed tRNA loops. Comparative genomic analyses identified TloR homologs across diverse bacterial lineages, where they are frequently embedded in conflict-associated loci. Structural modeling supports assignment of TloR to the recently described BECR-like superfamily, and mutational analyses identify conserved histidines required for toxicity and RNA cleavage. TloR cleaved tRNA and inhibited protein synthesis in a reconstituted translation system without detectable degradation of ribosomal RNA or plasmid DNA. Small-RNA sequencing showed that toxin-induced fragments arise from tRNAs decoding 19 of the 20 amino acids, with fragment endpoints strongly enriched near the anticodon loop. Purified TloR directly cleaved an unmodified tRNA substrate, predominantly within the anticodon loop. TloR therefore defines a family of BECR-like tRNases that combines broad tRNA recognition with positional preference for exposed tRNA loops. Together, these findings establish broad but positionally constrained tRNA cleavage as a distinct targeting strategy for antibacterial RNases.

papers.title: Testing the impact of gut microbiome rewilding on the health of captive bumble bees
papers.abstract: Animals and plants are often raised in captivity for food, companionship, conservation, or research purposes, a practice which typically reduces the diversity of their microbiomes. This loss of microbial diversity may in turn compromise host nutrition, pathogen resistance, and reproduction. Microbiome "rewilding"--restoring microbes present in the wild, but lost in captivity--has been proposed as a way to ameliorate these effects. However, it has only been tested in a handful of taxa. We evaluated the efficacy of microbiome rewilding in bumble bees (Bombus), a group of ecologically and agriculturally important pollinators. In captivity, bumble bees retain host-specialized "core" gut bacteria, but lack the diverse environmental bacteria commonly present in the gut of wild bees. We inoculated captive B. impatiens colonies with five species of environmental bacteria isolated from wild B. impatiens. Rewilding did not affect bee survival, reproduction, or nutrition (glycogen or lipid levels). We conducted a second experiment with Arsenophonus, the environmental bacterium exhibiting the highest colonization rate in captive bees, to test its role in resistance against an opportunistic bacterial pathogen. While inoculation with gut material from captive bees (which is dominated by core bacteria) completely protected hosts from pathogen infection, Arsenophonus inoculation had no effect. These findings demonstrate that microbiome rewilding is not always effective for sustaining the health of captive hosts.

papers.title: Role-Aware Line-Graph Neural Networks for Interpretable Prediction of Pairwise Microbial Interactions
papers.abstract: Predicting how microbial species affect each other's growth is a key challenge in microbial ecology. Using one of the largest available pairwise interaction datasets, comprising 20 soil bacteria co-cultured under 39 carbon conditions (15{,}074 directional measurements), we predicted whether one species has a positive or negative effect on the growth of another from monoculture growth, metabolic profiles, and phylogeny. Existing machine learning approaches treat each measurement as an independent sample, although experiments that share a species under the same condition are biologically related. We therefore represented the data as a role-aware line graph: each node is one directional measurement, and two nodes are connected when, under the same carbon condition, they share the same effector or the same affected species. This allows graph neural networks (GNNs) to pass information between related interactions. Our role-aware GAT-SAGE model achieved an F1-score of 81.38% for one-way prediction, outperforming the 73.79% previously reported for Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). For two-way interaction types (mutualism, competition, and parasitism), GAT-SAGE reached a macro F1-score of 60.34%. This exceeded the 55.71% of a neural network without graph structure but was below the 64.24% of XGBoost. Mutualism remained difficult to predict for all models. Layer-wise relevance propagation showed that one-way effects depend mainly on monoculture growth, whereas two-way interaction types depend more on the carbon environment. Encoding the dependency structure of interaction experiments thus adds information beyond the features of each measurement and provides interpretable insight into microbial interactions.

papers.title: Identification of three apicoplast transporters with crucial roles in the malaria parasite life cycle
papers.abstract: Malaria parasites depend on an intriguing endosymbiotic organelle, the apicoplast, for survival throughout the life cycle. The apicoplast is enclosed by four membranes and transport of metabolites across these membranes remains poorly understood. Thus far, only twelve (putative) membrane transport proteins have been confirmed to localize to the organelle. We report a crucial function in the apicoplast of three previously uncharacterized members of the major facilitator superfamily of transporters in Plasmodium falciparum. MCP1 and UMF are essential for asexual blood-stage parasites and could only be deleted in the presence of an alternative pathway for producing isopentenyl pyrophosphate. Deletion of either gene resulted in disruption of apicoplast morphology and loss of the organellar genome, suggesting that both are required for apicoplast housekeeping. In contrast, MCP2 was dispensable in the blood stages yet essential for parasite development in the mosquito. Oocysts in the mosquito midgut lacking MCP2 were significantly smaller than wild-type oocysts and produced no sporozoites, similar to when apicoplast fatty acid metabolism is disrupted. Differences in apicoplast morphology became apparent five days after infection, with MCP2-deficient oocyst apicoplasts displaying a less extended, sometimes fragmented, network with thinner branches. Taken together, we identified three novel apicoplast transporters, with MCP1 and UMF being essential for asexual blood-stage development by supporting apicoplast housekeeping, and MCP2 being crucial for parasite growth in mosquitoes, possibly by facilitating fatty acid metabolism.

papers.title: The blue dragon nudibranch (Glaucus atlanticus) shifts to less venomous prey in the Mediterranean, with no evidence of defensive microbial symbionts
papers.abstract: Glaucus atlanticus ("blue dragon"), is an aeolid nudibranch that acquires chemical defense through sequestration of nematocysts from its primary prey, the highly venomous Physalia physalis ("Portuguese man-of-war"). In August 2025 hundreds of G. atlanticus individuals appeared near Alicante (Spain), prompting temporary beach closures due to concerns about potential envenomation. This unusual occurrence, in a region where P. physalis is typically absent, raises questions about the trophic ecology and defensive strategies of this species under novel environmental conditions. Here, we used COI metabarcoding of gut to characterize the diet of G. atlanticus and combined it with 16S rRNA gene sequencing of cerata, gut, mucus, and central dorsal epidermis to assess potential microbial transfer from alternative prey that could contribute to the synthesis of defensive compounds, given that the role of microbes in chemical defense of aeolid nudibranchs was not assessed previously. We detected a trophic shift toward alternative cnidarian prey, including Pelagia noctiluca and Porpita porpita, which are not considered highly hazardous. Microbiome comparisons with P. porpita, as well as comparison of core microbiomes across different body parts of G. atlanticus, revealed no evidence of prey-derived transfer of mutualistic bacteria. Instead, G. atlanticus harbored distinct microbial communities dominated by environmentally widespread taxa, including potential opportunistic pathogens, with no indication of symbionts associated with defensive functions. Altogether, these findings indicate that, despite trophic flexibility, G. atlanticus may have limited capacity to maintain its defensive mechanisms in the absence of its primary prey.

papers.title: Bulk RNA-seq data of an Adherent-Invasive Escherichia coli Strain ZVL and Its exuR-Knockout Mutant
papers.abstract: Adherent-invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) is a subtype of pathogenic E. coli associated with Crohn's disease. AIEC strains are characterized by the ability to adhere to and invade epithelial cells, survive and replicate within macrophages. Despite many years of research, the mechanisms of virulence and pathogenicity still remain not fully understood. Previous studies have shown that the virulence-associated phenotype of some isolates can be reversibly eliminated by changing the growth medium, specifically by switching from M9 minimal medium supplemented with propionate to M9 supplemented with glucose. This phenomenon was also observed in ZVL, an AIEC isolate from our laboratory collection. Since certain sugar acids, particularly hexuronates, have been shown to contribute to gut colonization by other bacterial pathogens, their role in AIEC has not been reported in the literature. Therefore, we aimed to investigate whether the hexuronate degradation pathway influences the adhesion and invasion properties of AIEC. To this end, we generated a CRISPR-based deletion mutant lacking exuR, which encodes a transcriptional repressor of the Ashwell pathway, and performed bulk RNA sequencing of wild-type ZVL and the exuR mutant. Both strains were grown in M9 minimal medium supplemented with either glucose or sodium propionate. Caco-2 cell assays were used to assess bacterial adhesion and invasion under both growth conditions. Our results suggest that deletion of exuR affects the invasion phenotype following growth in propionate-supplemented medium.

papers.title: Pentose phosphate pathway metabolites are induced and required for nucleotides by latent Kaposi's Sarcoma infection of endothelial cells
papers.abstract: Kaposi's Sarcoma Herpesvirus (KSHV) is the etiologic agent of Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS). As a herpesvirus, KSHV has both latent and lytic phases and is predominantly found in the latent phase in KS spindle cells, the main proliferating cell of KS tumors. KS spindle cells express markers of endothelium. We previously found that latent KSHV infection of endothelial cells dramatically alters host cell metabolism including increased glucose uptake and glycolysis. The Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP), a shunt from glycolysis is often increased in cancer cells and some lytic viral infections. Here we found that KSHV increases intermediates of the oxidative half of the PPP in tert-immortalized microvascular endothelial cells. Chemical inhibition or knockout of an enzyme in the oxidative half of the PPP demonstrated the essential nature of the PPP during latent infection of endothelial cells. However, inhibition of the non-oxidative half has no effect on latently infected cells. The oxidative half of the PPP produces a substrate for nucleotide synthesis, ribose-5-phosphate. We found that both purine and pyrimidine synthesis are necessary for survival of KSHV latently infected endothelial cells but not for mock infected cells. Addition of exogenous ribose recovers much of the cell death induced by inhibition of the PPP, indicating that the PPP appears to be required for nucleotide synthesis. The requirement of nucleotide synthesis in latently infected cells raises the possibility that the PPP and nucleotides are needed for more than rapid viral replication during viral infection.

papers.title: An Oropouche virus N-glycosylation mutation in the Gc protein head domain is associated with transmissible infection in Anopheles mosquitoes
papers.abstract: The Oropouche virus (OROV) outbreak in South America raises concern about spreading to new foci. Although biting midges are primary OROV vectors in the Americas, we tested whether mutation and bottleneck selection could enable mosquito transmission. We used OROV240023 cultured in C6/36 cells to orally infect mosquito species. Infectious virus was detected in Aedes aegypti and Anopheles gambiae saliva, with the latter demonstrating faster dissemination at 7 days post-infection. Direct sequencing of virus from mosquito saliva identified a consensus nonsynonymous K614N substitution and a potential N-glycosylation site in the Gc glycoprotein involved in cell attachment. Bi-glycosylation of Gc has been reported for orthobunyaviruses infecting An. gambiae in East Africa. The K614N variant was a minor population (0.8%) in the input mosaic virus population used to infect mosquitoes. Virus isolated from mosquito saliva and subsequent C6/36 culture showed selection of the K614N variant. While the mechanism needs further elucidation, these findings suggest mosquito infection is possible, especially where vector populations are at higher density. Furthermore, the data warrant reconsideration of OROV240023 transmission risk beyond the Americas.

papers.title: Live vibratome sectioning of human lung and cerebral organoids for infection studies with respiratory and neurotropic viruses
papers.abstract: We present a robust, reproducible protocol for generating live, thin (300 micrometer) vibratome sections from human lung organoids and human cerebral organoids. The method preserves the native three-dimensional tissue architecture, cellular heterogeneity, and viability for at least 7 days in culture, providing a physiologically relevant platform for investigating respiratory and neurotropic virus infection. Following infection, samples can be fixed, cryoprotected, and embedded for downstream cryosectioning. These organoid sections support efficient analyses of viral entry, replication, and host responses. The technique is readily compatible with immunofluorescence, RNA in situ hybridization, spatial transcriptomics, live-cell imaging, and a wide range of advanced molecular and cellular assays. On average, five sections can be obtained from a single organoid, substantially increasing experimental throughput while reducing costs and biological variability. By combining the physiological complexity of three-dimensional organoid systems with the accessibility and scalability of tissue-section-based assays, this platform bridges a critical gap in respiratory and neuronal disease modeling. The protocol provides a versatile and high-resolution framework for studying respiratory and neurotropic viral pathogenesis, host-pathogen interactions, and therapeutic interventions in human lung as well as brain tissue.

papers.title: Cold atmospheric plasma for improved sustainability and fish welfare in recirculating aquaculture systems
papers.abstract: Decontamination of water is mandatory for the cultivation of aquatic species in recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). Avoiding economic and ecological losses while ensuring safe conditions is important for the future introduction of new technologies. Therefore, the implementation of cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) within RAS was examined for the first time. For the integration of this technology two equal RAS were set up, one using CAP, the other one ultraviolet light (UV) for water decontamination. Experiments with Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) were performed for three weeks to compare CAP with UV as reference. The CAP device was switched on intermittently for 8 hours daily (with intervals of 10 min on and 30 min off), while two UV lamps were turned on continuously throughout the entire time of 3 weeks, which required more energy. Fish development was tracked by fish weight and stress levels (cortisol measurements). Values for pH, conductivity, oxygen, temperature, microbial load, microbiome and ion composition were also monitored. Microbial loads for both setups were reduced by four orders of magnitude. The biodiversity of the microbiome of the two technologies was similar with a beta-diversity between 19 and 25. Deviations within each setup were low with the alpha-diversity ranging from 2.23-2.93 (CAP) and 2.42-2.79 (UV). The water monitoring revealed similar results for pH value, conductivity, oxygen and temperature. No differences for the cortisol measurements and also the fish weight were determined. The results demonstrate CAP as a competitive and more energy efficient alternative to UV benefiting fish welfare and development in a similar way. The equal development of fish and water parameters and low energy consumption compared to UV makes CAP an energy efficient tool, likewise enhancing fish welfare.
